title: Job 7:15–21
context: The speaker is Job, still addressing God. He says he would choose strangling and death rather than his present life, loathes his life, and asks God to leave him alone, for his days are a breath. He then asks what humanity is, that God should magnify it, set his mind on it, visit it each morning, and test it every moment, a question that echoes Psalm 8:4 and Psalm 144:3 but turns their praise into complaint. He asks how long God will not look away, and, while not admitting any specific guilt, asks why God does not simply pardon his sin before he lies down in the dust. Both traditions read Job’s death-wish language as honest anguish brought to God, not as counsel to act on; readers in similar darkness are encouraged to bring their lament to God, as Job does, and to seek help and care from others. Some translations render the end of 7:20 differently; the notes do not settle the wording and make no claim about manuscripts.

verses.text: so that my soul chooses strangling, death rather than my bones.
verses.arminianNotes: Job says his soul would choose strangling and death rather than his bones. Arminian readers see the depth of anguish, and read Job’s words as lament voiced to God, not as a course to follow.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Scripture giving honest voice to despair, and note that Job brings these feelings to God. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse pastorally, encouraging those in such darkness to seek God and the care of others.

verses.text: I loathe my life. I don’t want to live forever. Leave me alone, for my days are but a breath.
verses.arminianNotes: Job says he loathes his life and does not want to live forever, asking God to leave him alone. Arminian readers note that Job’s words come from exhaustion with suffering, voiced honestly before God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as genuine anguish, not a settled rejection of God. Both traditions read Job’s lament as within faith, and encourage sufferers who feel this way to bring it to God and to trusted people around them.

verses.text: What is man, that you should magnify him, that you should set your mind on him,
verses.arminianNotes: Job asks what man is, that God should magnify him and set his mind on him. Arminian readers note the echo of Psalm 8:4, where “what is man, that you think of him?” is a question of wonder and praise.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Job turns the same question into complaint, feeling God’s attention as oppressive rather than caring. Shared ground: both traditions name the echo and the inversion, without flattening Job’s lament into the psalm’s praise.

verses.text: that you should visit him every morning, and test him every moment?
verses.arminianNotes: Job says God visits him every morning and tests him every moment. Arminian readers see Job experiencing God’s attention as relentless scrutiny rather than comfort.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Psalm 144:3 asks a similar question in a different spirit, which Job’s words seem to turn around. Both traditions read Job’s complaint as honest, without reconciling it artificially with the psalms.

verses.text: How long will you not look away from me, nor leave me alone until I swallow down my spittle?
verses.arminianNotes: Job asks how long God will not look away or leave him alone even to swallow his spittle. Arminian readers note the vivid idiom for a moment’s respite, which Job feels he is denied.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear a man pleading for the briefest pause in what feels like unbroken scrutiny. Shared ground: this is lament, not accusation dressed as doctrine, and both traditions let it stand as Job says it.

verses.text: If I have sinned, what do I do to you, you watcher of men? Why have you set me as a mark for you, so that I am a burden to myself?
verses.arminianNotes: Job asks, if he has sinned, what harm it does to God, and why God has made him a target. Arminian readers note that Job does not admit specific guilt, but asks why any sin should warrant such affliction.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Job wrestling with how his suffering relates to his conduct, the very question his friends will answer too simply. Both traditions read the verse as Job’s honest question, not the book’s final verdict.

verses.text: Why do you not pardon my disobedience, and take away my iniquity? For now will I lie down in the dust. You will seek me diligently, but I will not be.”
verses.arminianNotes: Job asks why God does not pardon his disobedience and take away his iniquity before he dies. Arminian readers see a plea for forgiveness, even as Job maintains he does not know what he has done.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the plea a recognition that only God can pardon sin. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as honest lament, and note that the book later says Job spoke rightly of God (42:7), without treating that as a simple endorsement of every word.
